conversation.content:
Hello, I’m Dr. Martinez, a perinatal mental-health specialist. I’m here to help you settle into motherhood and to make sure you’re getting the support you need.  

Today we’ll use a short, well-studied questionnaire called the **EPDS**—the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale. It simply asks how you’ve been feeling emotionally over the past seven days. Your answers are completely confidential and will help us figure out the best next steps for your care. There are ten questions; we’ll go one at a time, and you can answer in your own words—no pressure to get anything “right.”  

Whenever you’re ready, we can begin.  

To start: In the past week, have you been able to laugh and see the funny side of things, or has that felt difficult?

Honestly? It’s been pretty hard. I used to laugh at little things all the time, but lately even the cute videos my sister sends feel flat. I’ll smile because I “should,” but genuine laughter feels… distant. Like I’m too tired or just can’t tap into that lightness right now.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things
Not really. I mean, I can force a chuckle if someone makes a joke, but it doesn’t feel natural or enjoyable—more like I’m just going through the motions.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

Not much. I used to get excited about little plans—grabbing coffee, even just a quiet shower—but right now it all feels like another chore. I’ll think “I should look forward to this,” but the spark isn’t there.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

Yeah… way too often. If the baby’s fussy, my brain jumps straight to “I’m doing something wrong” or “I’m a lousy mom.” I know rationally it’s not always my fault, but the guilt just shows up and sits on my chest.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

Pretty much every day. Even when everything looks fine—the baby’s breathing, the diapers are changed—I’ll suddenly feel this knot in my stomach like something bad is about to happen. I’ll check her a dozen times while she naps just to be sure.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

Yes. It’s like my heart will just start racing out of nowhere, and I get this wave of “what if something awful happens?” I haven’t had a full-blown panic attack, but a few times I’ve had to put the baby in the crib, step into the hallway, and breathe hard until the shaking stops.
Things have been getting on top of me

Most days, yeah. It feels like the laundry and bottles and night feeds just pile up faster than I can handle them. I’ll start one thing and remember two others and end up frozen, thinking, “How is everyone else doing this?”
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

A few nights, definitely. I’ll lie down exhausted, but my head keeps circling through “I’m failing her” or “what if she stops breathing,” and then I’m wide-awake for hours. Even when I do drift off, I wake up at every little grunt she makes.
I have felt sad or miserable
Yeah… pretty much every day this week. It’s like a gray cloud that settles in and won’t lift. I’ll be feeding her and tears just start dripping down my face, and I can’t even explain why.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying
Yes. It’s happened a few times—sometimes over something small like spilling pumped milk, sometimes over nothing I can name. The tears just come and I feel like I can’t stop them.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me
No, never. I’m exhausted and overwhelmed, but hurting myself hasn’t crossed my mind. I just want to feel better so I can take care of her.

stats.query:
postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 23: Screening Summary – Postpartum Visit  
Date: [today]

Patient endorsements (10-item EPDS responses, self-report):

1. Anhedonia: marked reduction in spontaneous laughter/pleasure.  
2. Loss of anticipatory enjoyment; activities perceived as burdensome.  
3. Excessive guilt/self-blame regarding infant care.  
4. Daily free-floating anxiety; intrusive “worst-case” thoughts.  
5. Episodic panic symptoms (tachycardia, trembling) without clear precipitant.  
6. Feeling overwhelmed by routine tasks; describes “freezing.”  
7. Mood-related insomnia—difficulty initiating and maintaining sleep despite fatigue.  
8. Persistent low mood reported “pretty much every day.”  
9. Frequent crying spells, sometimes without identifiable trigger.  
10. Denies any self-harm ideation.

Overall pattern: high endorsement of depressive and anxiety symptoms consistent with possible postpartum depression/anxiety.  
Safety: No self-harm thoughts reported. No current suicidality.

Screening significance: Total score 8 affirmative items (items 1-9), indicating elevated risk for postpartum mood disorder; warrants follow-up assessment and consideration of formal evaluation.
